This lecture was given as case-based teaching: each case below is from the course's 453 lecture file, written as the principle it teaches (black). Past-exam facts are in red.

The framework (summary case)

Use ABCDE; recognise shock and organ dysfunction early; resuscitate while diagnosing; identify the shock phenotype and the surgical source; obtain timely haemorrhage control or source control; reassess response continuously; and escalate early.
  • The sick surgical patient needs parallel processing: structured resuscitation, physiological interpretation, targeted investigation, definitive intervention, repeated reassessment, and multidisciplinary escalation.
  • Wrong approaches: "order tests first and intervene when certain", "treat hypotension with fluid in every patient", "focus only on the wound and drain", "a normal blood pressure rules out critical illness".
  • Primary survey order: Airway with C-spine precautions → Breathing → Circulation. 430

1. Recognising the deteriorating patient

  • Case: 72-year-old, 18 h after emergency right hemicolectomy for caecal perforation: confused, HR 118, BP 104/62, RR 30, T 38.2, SpO₂ 94% on 4 L, urine 15 mL/h, lactate 4.1 → organ dysfunction with likely shock. Activate urgent senior review and begin simultaneous ABCDE resuscitation, sepsis assessment and source evaluation (access, bloods/cultures, oxygen, antimicrobials, fluid-responsiveness, senior surgery/anaesthesia/ICU, decide on source control). Not: maintenance fluid and recheck in 4 h, paracetamol, CT after the round, furosemide.
  • A normal BP does not exclude shock: POD 2 after low anterior resection, lactate rising 2.2 → 4.7 despite 2 L, BP 108/68 → compensated shock; rising lactate means persistent hypoperfusion — look for bleeding, sepsis, bowel ischaemia, cardiac dysfunction, mixed shock.
  • MAP is a target, not proof: septic shock with MAP 70 on norepinephrine but mottled, oliguric, rising lactate → reassess macro/microcirculation, cardiac output, fluid responsiveness, source control. Capillary refill, skin, lactate trend, urine output and mental state all count.
  • Deterioration after an initial response → deliberate diagnostic reset: persistent contamination, missed ischaemia, occult haemorrhage, resistant infection, cardiogenic component, PE, line complication, alternative diagnosis.
  • Culture-negative sepsis is common — keep treating the syndrome while reassessing the source, antimicrobials and non-infectious causes.
  • Most accurate marker of inadequate tissue perfusion → lactate; best monitor of adequate resuscitation → urine output. 438 ×2 434 ×5 431 ×3
  • MAP = DBP + ⅓(SBP − DBP): BP 80/50 → 60. 438 ×2 437 Final
  • Hourly ICU monitoring essential: MAP. 439 ×2
  • Signs of shock are determined by the amount of intravascular volume lost. 431
  • Oliguria after only 350 cc in a 95 kg woman → inadequate resuscitation. 441
  • Fever, confusion, BP 80/50, lactate 4.5 → septic shock 441; flushed, hypotensive and confused POD 6 → septic shock. 430
  • SIRS: HR 110, RR 25, T 38.5, WBC 13,000 with normal BP → SIRS; HR is a SIRS criterion; T 38.4 + WBC 14,000 supports SIRS; organ dysfunction → "severe sepsis". 442 432 ×3 441 432 ×2
  • The SIRS-in-ICU question keyed gastroduodenal (stress) ulcer as the supporting finding. 441
  • Long critical illness (necrotizing pancreatitis on ventilator/inotropes): stress response → insulin resistance and ↑ glucagon (keys differ: 434 = glucagon, 433 = insulin). 434 433
  • Persistent hyperglycemia on TPN despite insulin → look for sepsis. 438 ×4 435 Final

2. Shock phenotypes

PhenotypeClues from the lecture cases
Haemorrhagic/hypovolaemicCool peripheries, narrow pulse pressure, falling Hb, abdominal distension, positive FAST
Distributive (septic)Warm peripheries, bounding pulses, low systemic vascular tone (early)
CardiogenicCrackles, raised JVP, cool peripheries after fluid in IHD
ObstructiveTension pneumothorax (absent breath sounds, distended neck veins); PE (dilated RV, septal flattening); tamponade
MixedCommon in surgical patients — never use one sign alone to exclude haemorrhage or sepsis
  • Persistent shock after initial resuscitation needs phenotyping: dynamic fluid-responsiveness tests and focused echocardiography (persistent preload responsiveness, vasoplegia, ventricular dysfunction, tamponade, right-heart strain). Static indices like CVP alone are unreliable.
  • 78-year-old with IHD, hypotensive after 2 L for sepsis, now crackles + raised JVP → mixed septic + cardiogenic shock; more fluid may harm.
  • Severe heart failure + sepsis → cautious, reassessed fluid challenges, early vasopressors if needed.
  • Severe aortic stenosis + sepsis → maintain coronary perfusion pressure, avoid severe tachycardia and fluid overload.
  • Vasopressors: norepinephrine can run through a good peripheral line temporarily — don't delay it for central access.
  • Indicator of ICU need: persistent hypotension needing vasopressors after initial resuscitation (also rising O₂ needs, altered consciousness, worsening acidosis/lactate).
  • Arterial line: beat-to-beat pressure and repeated blood sampling in unstable shock/vasopressor use — it doesn't measure volume or replace examination.
  • Tension pneumothorax → obstructive shock. 442 434
  • Hypotension + bradycardia + warm extremities after trauma (spinal injury) → neurogenic shock 438 ×9 430; treat with IV fluids + vasopressors. 426
  • Same picture but with tachycardia (HR 120) — the compilers note this doesn't fit neurogenic shock (which has bradycardia). 432
  • Septic shock = systemic vasodilation (↓ SVR), collapsed IVC, hyperdynamic LV; peripheral vasodilation; microcirculatory dysfunction. 442 432 ×5 431 ×2
  • Anterior MI with BP 80/50 (cardiogenic shock) → normal intravascular volume 431 ×3; chest pain + hypotension POD 1 → cardiogenic shock. 430
  • Anaphylaxis to IV contrast (bradycardia, hypotension) → intravascular volume redistribution (vasodilation, leak). 431 ×2
  • Tamponade vs tension pneumothorax: the differentiating sign is breath sounds (both have raised JVP and hypotension). 438 ×3
  • Collapse in recovery 1 h after appendectomy → hypovolemic shock (bleeding) 431 ×3; bleeding, aspiration and PE are causes — wound abscess is NOT (too early). 426
  • Tachycardia + low urine output after sleeve gastrectomy → leak. 436
  • Resuscitated trauma patient: class II hemorrhage = HR 100–120, normal SBP, RR 20–30 (BP 100/60, HR 110). 430

3. Haemorrhage

  • Blunt trauma, HR 132, BP 88/54, positive FAST, transient response → immediate transfer to theatre for haemorrhage control (laparotomy). CT is for stable patients; vasopressors don't replace haemorrhage control.
  • Concealed bleeding: hypotension 6 h after lap chole, Hb 12.6 → 8.8, distension, drain only 30 mL → concealed intra-abdominal haemorrhage — drains can block or not communicate. Treat as haemorrhage until proved otherwise.
  • Anticoagulated patient with retroperitoneal haemorrhage → resuscitate, reverse anticoagulation, activate blood products, arrange IR or surgical control.
  • Lethal cycle: hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy + hypocalcaemia (T 34, pH 7.16, low ionised Ca) = trauma-induced coagulopathy → haemorrhage control, warming, balanced products, calcium, minimal crystalloid.
  • Damage-control resuscitation: avoid large crystalloid volumes (dilute clotting factors, worsen hypothermia/acidosis, dislodge clots); permissive hypotension is NOT for traumatic brain injury.
  • Pelvic gunshot, unstable, negative FAST → preperitoneal pelvic packing + stabilisation, angioembolisation for persistent arterial bleeding. A negative FAST doesn't exclude retroperitoneal pelvic bleeding; laparotomy without an intraperitoneal indication can release pelvic tamponade.
  • TBI + haemorrhagic shock: prevent hypoxaemia and hypotension (protect cerebral perfusion) while doing damage-control haemorrhage management; brief hyperventilation only as rescue; mannitol/hypertonic not routinely.
  • Diffuse oozing after massive transfusion with fibrinogen 0.9 g/L → fibrinogen replacement (cryoprecipitate/concentrate), correct hypocalcaemia, rewarm. Fibrinogen is often the first factor to fall; replace if ≤ 1.5 g/L. TXA early (within 3 h of injury) without waiting for tests.
  • Massive transfusion ratio PRBC : plasma : platelets = 1 : 1 : 1. 442
  • Warfarin with active bleeding and instability → stop warfarin, IV vitamin K + FFP (or PCC). 442
  • Oozing from lines after 6 units, low platelets, prolonged PT/PTT → give FFP next. 441 ×2
  • Bleeding from cannula sites, prolonged PT/PTT, low platelets, high degradation products → DIC → D-dimer. 438 ×7
  • Massive transfusion complications: hyperkalemia, citrate toxicity (hypocalcemia), hypothermia, coagulopathy. 431 ×2 431 ×3
  • Gram-negative bacteremia after splenic rupture + transfusion → bacterial translocation from the bowel. 432 ×2
  • Fever, chest tightness, pain at the infusion site, hypotension, dark urine during transfusion → acute hemolytic transfusion reaction. 437 ×4 431 ×2
  • Stab wound, unconscious, BP 70/40 (class IV) → first endotracheal intubation (airway). 432 ×4
  • Conscious trauma patient, BP 75/45, on O₂ → next two large-bore IV lines. 431
  • Trauma patient BP 88/56, HR 121, talking → 1 L bolus of RL 438 ×7; resuscitation fluid → Ringer's lactate. 441 434 ×2 431 ×3
  • Hyperchloremic acidosis after resuscitation → bolus Ringer's lactate. 430
  • Fastest access in an adult trauma with difficult IV access → intraosseous. 432 ×2
  • Upper GI bleed (variceal or ulcer): airway first if GCS is low, then crystalloid resuscitation, then endoscopy. 438 ×3 438 ×5 431 430 430
  • Egyptian patient (old bilharziasis), hematemesis, HR 110, BP 100/65, ascites + splenomegaly (variceal bleed) → first IV fluid resuscitation. 429 Final

4. Sepsis & source control

  • Generalised peritonitis with shock (perforated diverticulitis) → urgent source control once resuscitation is underway — resuscitation runs simultaneously, not as a reason for delay. Source control = control contamination, drain infected fluid, debride non-viable tissue, address the lesion.
  • Anastomotic leak (faeculent drain, pelvic collection with extravasation) → urgent senior review for source control: drainage, diversion or reoperation. Antibiotics are necessary but insufficient.
  • Perforated peptic ulcer, now more stable → still needs definitive source control — the hole keeps contaminating.
  • Severe cholangitis → after resuscitation and antibiotics, urgent biliary decompression (ERCP).
  • Persistent septic shock after a drain → reassess source control (undrained locules, ongoing leak, necrosis); drain placement ≠ adequate drainage.
  • Percutaneous drainage suits a well-defined accessible abscess in a stable patient without generalised peritonitis; diffuse peritonitis, uncontrolled contamination, ischaemia or deterioration need surgery.
  • Mesenteric ischaemia with lactate 6.5, acidosis and peritonism → urgent surgical/vascular assessment, revascularisation and/or laparotomy.
  • SBO with fever, tachycardia, acidosis and localised peritonism → presume strangulation until excluded.
  • Necrotising pancreatitis: sterile necrosis doesn't automatically need intervention; deterioration → assess organ failure and intra-abdominal hypertension.
  • Fever, hiccups and tachycardia after sleeve gastrectomy → CT for leak/abscess. 437
  • Severe pancreatitis: generalized edema despite fluids → third-space losses. 438 ×3 432 ×4
  • Pneumonia patient on 3 vasopressors who becomes anuric → non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia (NOMI) (keyed). 439
  • ICU septic shock + sudden abdominal pain, distension, lactic acidosis → non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia. 442 Final
  • ICU patient (ventilated > 48 h, on vasopressors) bleeding from the NG tube → prevent with gastric acid suppression (stress ulcer prophylaxis). 439

5. Respiratory deterioration

  • Opioid-induced hypercapnic failure (drowsy, RR 8, PCO₂ 9 kPa, pH 7.21) → support airway and ventilation, stop opioids/sedatives, titrated naloxone. Oxygen alone may hide rising CO₂.
  • Tiring septic patient (RR 38, PCO₂ rising 4.2 → 5.8, mental state worse) → impending ventilatory failure — escalate for airway support.
  • Tension pneumothorax after subclavian line → immediate decompression before the chest X-ray.
  • Post-op PE: sudden hypoxaemia + hypotension with dilated RV and septal flattening → obstructive shock. Stable with high suspicion → CT pulmonary angiography (D-dimer is unhelpful post-op). Unstable with RV strain → supportive resuscitation, senior MDT input, assess bleeding risk for reperfusion; avoid large fluid volumes.
  • Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: frothy sputum, crackles, hypertension, B-lines.
  • Induction of anaesthesia in shock risks cardiovascular collapse and aspiration; peri-intubation hypotension = loss of sympathetic tone, vasodilatation and reduced venous return from positive pressure.
  • GCS ≤ 8 → intubate (GCS 6 or 7 trauma patient). 431 439
  • Just intubated → sudden desaturation, absent breath sounds on the RIGHT, high peak airway pressure → right tension pneumothorax (a tube in the right main bronchus silences the LEFT side). 442 Final
  • Unconscious trauma patient not moving limbs (possible C-spine) → open the airway with a jaw thrust (no head tilt) 438 ×3 432 ×3; stridor and SpO₂ 88% after a fall → in-line immobilisation + definitive airway. 438 ×6
  • Respiratory distress after extubation (accessory muscles, paradoxical breathing, confusion) → reintubate immediately. 439
  • Drowsy in recovery with SpO₂ 90% and normal pulse/BP → respiratory failure (residual anaesthetic/opioids). 430
  • Excess opiates → high PaCO₂ (respiratory acidosis). 431 ×3
  • Emphysema + hematemesis, pH 7.23, PO₂ 42, PCO₂ 75, confused → intubate and ventilate (426 key: correct hypoxia with O₂). 430 ×2 426
  • Hard to bag, reduced air entry left, trachea to the right → needle decompression, left 2nd intercostal space. 430
  • Hypotension and desaturation 2 h after a subclavian line → tension pneumothorax 438 ×3; convulsion is not a central-line complication (arrhythmia, air embolism, hematoma are). 426
  • Post-op chest pain, dyspnea, hypotension, normal ECG/enzymes (POD 5 after APR) → CT chest (CTPA) for PE 438 ×9; massive PE with BP responding to fluid → LMWH (keyed). 430
  • HR 160, BP 90/60 a day after lung resection → atrial fibrillation. 439
  • VAP prevention → daily sedation hold / extubation trials 439; most common ICU infection in burns → VAP. 442

6. Abdominal compartment syndrome

  • Tense distended abdomen + new organ dysfunction (oliguria, rising airway pressures, impaired venous return, shock) = intra-abdominal hypertension / ACS: escalate, measure bladder pressure, improve wall compliance, decompress (surgically if needed).
  • After damage-control laparotomy: rising vasopressors, lactate 4 → 8, pH 7.18, urine 5 mL/h, rising airway pressures, tense abdomen and a hyperdynamic underfilled LV → ACS → urgent decompression/relook; minimal drain output doesn't exclude it.
  • After damage control, worsening acidosis, lactate, vasopressors and abdominal effluent → concern for ongoing pathology → relook.
  • Post-op oliguria with a blocked catheter → restore drainage first, while still assessing perfusion.
  • Persistent ICP 28–30 despite basic measures in TBI → intermittent hyperosmolar therapy and reassess; no prolonged hyperventilation; don't lower MAP.
  • Intra-abdominal pressure 32 mmHg with oliguria and rising ventilatory pressures → abdominal compartment syndrome. 442

7. ICU admission (from past exams)

  • Most benefit from ICU: young polytrauma with head and trunk injuries (not the uncomplicated lap chole or palliative stage-4 cancer). 438 437 Final
  • Stable patient with grade 4 liver laceration + small SDH → ICU for hemodynamic and neuro-vitals monitoring. 437 436
  • Unstable patient after emergency surgery for perforated DU → ICU admission reduces morbidity. 438
  • Obese patient with difficult closure and congested bowel after resection → ICU monitoring (ACS risk). 439
  • Real-time (beat-to-beat) BP monitoring → arterial line in the radial artery. 437 ×3
  • Clinical brain death: GCS 3 with no gag, corneal or cough reflex, no pupil response and no breathing (apnoea). Any reflex or any breathing excludes it. 436 Final ×2

Metabolic (stress) response to injury (from past exams)

Goes UPGoes DOWN
Catecholamines, cortisol (ACTH from the anterior pituitary), glucagonInsulin (relative deficiency + insulin resistance → hyperglycaemia)
Growth hormone, ADH, aldosterone, prolactinT3, testosterone/sex hormones
Cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) → fever, acute-phase proteins
  • After splenectomy for trauma, the hormone expected to be low → insulin. 432
  • Splenectomy + femur fixation → increased growth hormone (cortisol up, ADH up, hyperglycaemia — not the opposite). 431 ×3
  • The metabolic response to injury includes an increase in ADH secretion (ACTH comes from the pituitary, not the hypothalamus; GH rises; glucose rises). 430
  • Endocrine response after an operation — two versions with different keys: 438 Final keyed "increase in anabolic hormones" 438 Final; 431 Midterm keyed "increasing the function of all endocrine glands". 431 Learn the stress-hormone rise and insulin fall above.
  • 60% burn — activation of the metabolic response → local vasodilation via nitric oxide (the source marked B and D with "??"). 430
  • Oxygen–haemoglobin curve: left shift = cold, ↓2,3-DPG, alkalosis, CO-Hb, fetal Hb. Fever and ↑2,3-DPG shift it RIGHT → both are the "except" answers (keyed A and D). 426

8. Other emergencies (from past exams)

  • Anaphylaxis (urticaria + wheeze after contrast, or sting with drooling/hypotension) → epinephrine (IM 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000). 436 ×9 426 431
  • Anaphylaxis on starting penicillin → stop the drug first 435 ×6; sudden wheeze, cyanosis and hypotension after antibiotics → anaphylactic shock. 430
  • Malignant hyperthermia (hypercarbia, rigidity, rising temperature after volatiles + succinylcholine) → IV dantrolene + supportive care. 442
  • Expanding neck hematoma with stridor after thyroidectomy → open the wound and evacuate the hematoma at the bedside immediately (keyed B). 442
  • Tetanus → airway and ventilation first. 430 ×2
  • Hyperkalemia with ECG changes → calcium first. 434 ×6 429
  • High-AG acidosis from severe hemorrhage (lactic). 432 ×2
dug:
Shock

Hypovolemic shock:
  • Hypovolemic shock occurs due to inadequate circulating blood volume, leading to decreased organ perfusion and oxygen delivery.
  • Causes include:
  • Bleeding (most common cause)
  • Severe vomiting or diarrhea
  • Fluid sequestration in the gut (e.g., bowel obstruction, burns)
Physiologic Compensation Mechanisms

The body compensates for hypovolemia through the adrenergic nervous system, which:

1. Constricts veins & venules, shifting blood toward the heart.

2. Constricts arterioles in non-essential organs (skin, muscle, gut, liver),

  • preserving blood flow to the brain & heart.

3. Increases heart rate & contractility to improve cardiac output.

4. Stimulates sodium & water retention via the renin-angiotensin-

  • aldosterone system and vasopressin release, helping to restore blood
  • volume.
Signs & Symptoms of Hypovolemic Shock
  • Early Signs:
  • Cool skin, delayed capillary refill (most sensitive early sign).
  • Difficult IV access due to vasoconstriction.
  • Orthostatic hypotension (SBP drop >20 mmHg or DBP drop >10 mmHg upon standing).
  • Oliguria (urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h in adults, <1 mL/kg/h in children, <2 mL/kg/h in infants).
  • Moderate Shock (20–30% blood loss):
  • Thirst & hypotension (even in supine position).
  • Metabolic acidosis due to anaerobic metabolism.
  • Severe Shock (>30% blood loss):
  • Profound hypotension and altered mental status (agitation, confusion, lethargy).
  • Myocardial ischemia (ST-T segment changes, arrhythmias).
  • Metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis post-resuscitation).
Diagnostic Pitfalls
  • Normal blood pressure does NOT rule out shock.
  • Heart rate is unreliable (some patients may have normal HR or even bradycardia in severe cases).
  • Mental status changes can mimic intoxication (shock must be ruled out before assuming drug/alcohol intoxication).
  • Cutaneous vasoconstriction may be masked by alcohol, vasodilators, or sedatives.
Laboratory & Monitoring Clues
  • Hematocrit falls within minutes if IV fluids are given, but may take hours without fluids.
  • A Hct drop of 3–4% suggests ~10% blood loss, while 6–8% suggests ~20% blood loss (~1 L in adults).
  • Bladder catheterization is essential to monitor urine output.

Management

A. Airway and Ventilation
  • Priority: Secure the airway immediately, especially in severe shock.
  • Preemptive Intubation & Mechanical Ventilation:
  • Ensure adequate oxygenation and ventilation.
  • Prevents emergency intubation under unstable conditions.
  • Volume-Control Ventilation: Preferred in initial resuscitation.
  • Risks of Positive-Pressure Ventilation in Hypovolemia:
  • Compresses vena cava → Reduces venous return → Worsens hypotension.
  • Increases pulmonary vascular resistance → Impairs right heart function.
  • Reduces left atrial filling → Limits cardiac output.
  • Can lead to cardiovascular collapse if intubation is performed without fluid resuscitation.
  • Preparation for Possible Collapse: In emergency settings, teams must anticipate and prepare for sudden deterioration upon intubation.
B. Bleeding Control
1. External Bleeding:
  • Direct Pressure is the first step.
  • Tourniquets for extremity bleeding (safe for ≤2 hours).
  • Hemostatic Agents (commercially available, FDA-approved).
2. Internal Bleeding:
  • Chest Bleeding: Place a chest tube to drain blood, re-expand the lung, and monitor for ongoing hemorrhage.
  • Pelvic Fracture: Apply a pelvic binder; definitive control via angiographic embolization or surgery.
  • Long-Bone Fractures: Immobilization reduces further bleeding.
  • Abdominal or Thoracic Bleeding: Immediate surgical intervention is required.
3. Avoid Blind Clamping:
  • Risks: Can injure vessels and cause further bleeding.
C. Initial Fluid Resuscitation
1. Vascular Access
  • Large-bore IV access (16G or larger) via:
  • Peripheral veins (upper extremities)
  • Central veins (jugular, subclavian, femoral) with ultrasound guidance
  • Saphenous vein cutdown
  • Intraosseous (sternum, tibia, humerus) if IV access fails
2. Crystalloid Resuscitation (1-2 L Bolus Initially)
  • Options:
  • Normal saline (NS) – Preferred if pH > 7.2.
  • Lactated Ringer’s (LR) – Used if severe acidosis (pH < 7.2) due to buffering effects.
  • Avoid LR in liver disease (inadequate lactate metabolism).
  • Caution:
  • Excess crystalloids can lead to dilutional coagulopathy and tissue edema.
  • If no response after 1-2 L of crystalloids, initiate blood transfusion.
D. Blood Product Transfusion
1. Indications for PRBC Transfusion:
  • >1.5 L blood loss (~30% of blood volume lost)
  • Earlier transfusion if:
  • Ongoing bleeding.
  • Preexisting coronary artery disease.
2. Emergency Transfusion Protocols:
  • Unmatched Type-O PRBCs: Used initially.
  • Rh-positive PRBCs for men and postmenopausal women.
  • Rh-negative PRBCs for women of childbearing age.
  • Type-Specific Blood: Can be given within 10 minutes.
3. Massive Transfusion Protocol (≥6 PRBCs Given):
  • 1:1:1 Ratio of PRBCs, Plasma, and Platelets
  • Prevents dilutional coagulopathy.
  • Improves oxygen delivery & hemostasis.
  • Avoids excessive crystalloid infusion.
E. Goals of Fluid Resuscitation
  • Avoid excessive fluids: Over-resuscitation leads to tissue edema, impairing organ function and wound healing.
  • Avoid under-resuscitation: Inadequate resuscitation increases the risk of multi-organ failure.
  • Targeted Resuscitation Goals:
  • Systolic BP of 80 mmHg (radial pulse present) until bleeding is controlled.
  • Systolic BP of 90 mmHg post-bleeding control.
  • Higher BP targets for elderly patients to ensure brain and cardiac perfusion.
  • Clinical indicators of adequate resuscitation:
  • Improved skin perfusion (warm, rapid capillary refill).
  • Urine output >0.5 mL/kg/hr in adults, >1 mL/kg/hr in children.
  • Improved mental status.
  • Normalization of acid-base balance (resolving metabolic acidosis).
  • Pitfalls:
  • BP alone is not a reliable marker due to compensatory vasoconstriction.
  • Ethanol or sedatives may interfere with compensatory responses.
  • Pain-induced hypertension should not be mistaken for normovolemia.
F. Correction of Coagulation Abnormalities
  • Trauma and sepsis often lead to coagulopathy with:
  • Prolonged clotting times (PT, aPTT).
  • Low platelets and fibrinogen.
  • Elevated fibrin degradation products.
  • Treatment strategies:
  • Plasma (FFP or pre-thawed plasma) for low clotting factors.
  • Platelets for counts <50,000 in active bleeding or <100,000 in head trauma.
  • Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC):
    • Rapidly reverses warfarin-related coagulopathy.
    • Reduces need for high-volume plasma transfusions.
  • Tranexamic Acid (TXA):
    • Prevents excessive fibrinolysis.
    • Effective if given within 3 hours of hemorrhage.
    • Thromboelastography (TEG) can guide TXA use.
  • Prehospital Plasma (PAMPer Trial):
  • ~10% mortality reduction in hemorrhagic shock patients.
  • Plasma use before hospital arrival improves survival.
G. Hypothermia: Prevention & Treatment
  • Hypothermia worsens coagulopathy → Increased bleeding risk.
  • Causes:
  • Blood loss → Reduced metabolic heat production.
  • Cold IV fluids and blood products.
  • Environmental exposure (trauma, surgery).
  • Preventive Strategies:
  • Keep operating room & resuscitation areas warm.
  • Use warmed IV fluids and blood products.
  • Minimize skin exposure during resuscitation.
  • Apply forced-air warming blankets (e.g., Bair Hugger).
  • Active Rewarming Methods:
  • Forced-air warming devices (most effective).
  • Heated IV fluids/blood products.
  • Warm blankets and head coverings.
  • Core warming via heated humidified oxygen.
  • Extracorporeal warming may be required for severe hypothermia (<32°C).
H. Modalities to Avoid
1. Colloids (e.g., Hetastarch, Dextran, Albumin)
  • No proven benefit over crystalloids.
  • Increase cost without improving survival.
  • May cause renal dysfunction and coagulopathy (Hetastarch).
  • Used only in mass casualty or battlefield scenarios when crystalloid volume is limited.
2. Vasopressors in Hypovolemia
  • Should NOT be used in hemorrhagic shock unless necessary.
  • Risk of ischemic complications:
  • Gut necrosis.
  • Limb ischemia and gangrene.
  • Acute kidney injury.
  • Liver failure.
  • Exception:
  • Temporary use in refractory shock while initiating aggressive volume resuscitation.
Cardiac Compressive (Obstructive) Shock:

Cardiac compressive shock occurs when external pressure on the heart or great veins impairs venous return and cardiac output. Common causes include:

1. Pericardial Tamponade
  • Fluid accumulation in the pericardial sac compresses the heart.
  • Beck's Triad:
    • Hypotension
    • Distended neck veins (JVD)
    • Muffled heart sounds
  • Pulsus paradoxus: Decrease in systolic BP >10 mmHg during inspiration (key diagnostic feature).
  • ECG: Electrical alternans (alternating QRS amplitude).

2. Tension Pneumothorax

  • Air trapped in the pleural space creates positive pressure, collapsing the lung and shifting mediastinal structures.
  • Signs:
    • Tracheal deviation (away from affected side)
    • Absent breath sounds on affected side
    • JVD and hypotension
  • CXR: Mediastinal shift and lung collapse.

3. Massive Hemothorax

  • Accumulation of blood (>1.5 L) in the pleural cavity impairs cardiac filling.
  • Signs:
    • Shock + Absent breath sounds + Dullness to percussion
    • JVD may be present in non-hypovolemic patients.
  • CXR: Large radio-opaque hemothorax.

4. Diaphragmatic Rupture with Herniation

  • Abdominal organs move into the thoracic cavity, compressing the heart.
  • Signs:
    • Dyspnea, bowel sounds in chest, epigastric pain.
  • CXR: Bowel loops in thorax, elevated hemidiaphragm.

5. Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS)

  • Severe intra-abdominal hypertension (>20 mmHg) compresses the IVC, reducing venous return and cardiac output.
  • Signs:
    • Tense, distended abdomen
    • Oliguria and high peak airway pressures (if ventilated)
  • Measurement: Bladder pressure (>20 mmHg) confirms ACS.
Treatment
1. Immediate Fluid Resuscitation (Bridging Strategy)
  • Bolus of IV fluids to improve venous return and transiently relieve compression.
  • Avoid excessive fluids to prevent worsening cardiac dysfunction.
2. Definitive Mechanical Correction
  • Pericardial Tamponade → Pericardiocentesis or Surgical Pericardial Window
  • US-guided pericardiocentesis is first-line for unstable patients.
  • Pericardial window in trauma or recurrent cases.
  • Tension Pneumothorax → Needle Decompression & Chest Tube
  • Needle decompression: 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line (quickest).
  • Chest tube insertion: 5th intercostal space, midaxillary line.
  • Massive Hemothorax → Tube Thoracostomy & Surgery
  • Chest tube drainage (if >1.5 L or >200 mL/hr, immediate surgery needed).
  • Diaphragmatic Herniation → Urgent Surgery
  • Laparotomy or thoracotomy for visceral reduction and diaphragm repair.
  • Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS) → Surgical Decompression
  • Bladder pressure monitoring guides intervention.
  • Emergent laparotomy if ACS confirmed.
Cardiogenic Shock:

Cardiogenic shock is caused by severe heart failure, leading to inadequate cardiac output and end-organ hypoperfusion. It can result from:

1. Myocardial Causes
  • Acute Myocardial Infarction (AMI) (most common)
  • Myocarditis
  • Cardiomyopathies (e.g., dilated, hypertrophic)
  • Ventricular aneurysm
  • Takotsubo cardiomyopathy

2. Mechanical Causes

  • Valvular disease (acute mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis)
  • Ventricular septal rupture
  • Papillary muscle rupture (post-MI)
  • Pericardial tamponade

3. Arrhythmic Causes

  • Bradyarrhythmias (severe sinus bradycardia, complete heart block)
  • Tachyarrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response)
Clinical Presentation
  • Hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg or MAP < 65 mmHg)
  • Cold, clammy extremities (poor perfusion)
  • Tachycardia (except in bradyarrhythmic causes)
  • Pulmonary congestion (if LV failure):
  • Dyspnea, crackles, pulmonary edema
  • JVD & peripheral edema (if RV failure)
  • Altered mental status, oliguria (low urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/hr)
Diagnosis
  • Hemodynamic Criteria for Cardiogenic Shock
  • SBP < 90 mmHg (for >30 min)
  • Cardiac index < 2.2 L/min/m²
  • Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) > 18 mmHg
  • Elevated lactate > 2 mmol/L (tissue hypoxia)
Diagnostic Workup
  • ECG: ST-elevation MI (STEMI), arrhythmias
  • Echocardiography: Evaluates LV function, valve disease, tamponade
  • Pulmonary artery catheter (Swan-Ganz): Confirms low cardiac index & high PCWP
  • Cardiac enzymes (troponin, BNP): Detects myocardial injury or overload
  • Chest X-ray: Pulmonary congestion, enlarged heart
  • ABG/Lactate: Metabolic acidosis & tissue hypoperfusion
Management
A. Immediate Stabilization
1. Airway & Breathing
  • Oxygen, Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) if mild
  • Intubation & mechanical ventilation if severe pulmonary edema
  • Avoid excessive positive-pressure ventilation (reduces preload)

2. Circulatory Support

  • IV Fluids (cautiously!)
    • Small 250-500 mL boluses ONLY if hypovolemia
  • Vasopressors (if MAP < 65 mmHg)
    • First-line: Norepinephrine
    • Alternative: Dopamine (for bradycardia-related shock)
  • Inotropes (if CO is low)
    • Dobutamine (increases contractility)
    • Milrinone (for patients on beta-blockers)
  • Diuretics (if pulmonary edema)
    • Furosemide 20-40 mg IV (if volume overload)
B. Targeted Therapies Based on Cause
CauseTreatment
STEMI/NSTEMIUrgent PCI or CABG
Valvular DiseaseSurgery (valve repair/replacement)
Ventricular Septal RuptureEmergency surgery
TamponadePericardiocentesis
ArrhythmiasCardioversion (if unstable), antiarrhythmics
Severe LV DysfunctionMechanical circulatory support (IABP, ECMO)
C. Advanced Therapies
1. Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (IABP)
  • Improves coronary perfusion and reduces afterload
  • Use in: Acute MI, severe LV failure

2. Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO)

  • Temporary biventricular support
  • Indications: Cardiogenic shock not responding to vasopressors/inotropes

3. Ventricular Assist Device (VADs)

  • Used as bridge to heart transplantation
  • Considered in end-stage heart failure
Neurogenic Shock:

Neurogenic shock occurs due to failure of the autonomic nervous system, leading to loss of vascular tone and severe hypotension. It results from:

1. Spinal Cord Injury (SCI)
  • Above T6 → Sympathetic denervation → Profound hypotension & bradycardia
  • Below T6 → Hypotension with compensatory tachycardia

2. Anesthetic Causes

  • Spinal or epidural anesthesia (blocking sympathetic outflow)
  • General anesthesia with excessive vasodilation
3. Pharmacologic Causes
  • Autonomic blocking agents (e.g., alpha- or beta-blockers)

4. Trauma & Brain Injury

  • Brainstem trauma affecting sympathetic output
Clinical Features
  • Hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg, MAP < 65 mmHg)
  • Bradycardia (HR < 60 bpm) if lesion above T6
  • Warm, flushed skin below injury level (vasodilation)
  • Decreased cardiac output & stroke volume
  • Neurologic deficits (paralysis, sensory loss, areflexia in SCI)
Key Differentiation:
  • Spinal Cord Injury → Neurogenic Shock (Hypotension + Bradycardia)
  • Head Trauma → NOT Neurogenic Shock (Cushing’s Reflex: HTN + Bradycardia)
Diagnosis
TestFindings
ECGSinus bradycardia (if high spinal lesion)
FAST ultrasoundRules out hemorrhagic shock
Spinal MRI/CTConfirms spinal cord injury
Hemodynamics↓ SVR, ↓ CVP, ↓ MAP, ↓ CO
ABG/LactateMetabolic acidosis (if severe shock)
Management
A. Immediate Stabilization
1. Airway & Breathing
  • If high cervical injury (C3-C5) → Intubate! (Diaphragmatic paralysis)
  • Spinal immobilization to prevent further injury
  • Oxygen therapy

2. Circulatory Support

  • IV Fluids (First-Line)
    • Start with 1-2 L of isotonic crystalloid (LR or NS)
    • Monitor MAP (goal > 85-90 mmHg for spinal cord perfusion)
  • Vasopressors (if fluids are insufficient)
    • Norepinephrine (First-line if bradycardia)
    • Phenylephrine (If HR is normal or high)
    • Dopamine (If bradycardia + hypotension)
B. Supportive & Definitive Therapy
1. Positioning
  • Trendelenburg position (if no contraindications) to improve venous return
  • Spinal immobilization (cervical collar, backboard)

2. Neuroprotection & ICU Monitoring

  • Monitor for secondary spinal cord injury
  • MAP goal: 85-90 mmHg for at least 7 days (to prevent spinal ischemia)
  • Foley catheter to monitor urine output

3. Atropine (For Severe Bradycardia)

  • 0.5 mg IV, repeat every 3-5 min (max: 3 mg total)
  • Consider transcutaneous pacing if refractory

4. DVT Prophylaxis (Due to prolonged immobility)

  • LMWH or Heparin

Low-output Inflammatory (Septic) shock:

Inflammatory shock (also known as septic shock) occurs due to systemic inflammation that leads to vascular dysfunction and hypoperfusion. It can result from:

  • Intra-abdominal sepsis (bowel perforation, ischemia, necrosis, abscesses,
  • peritonitis)
  • Soft tissue infections (necrotizing fasciitis, gangrene, infected burns)
  • Ischemia-reperfusion injury (massive trauma, inadequate resuscitation)
  • Inflammatory shock mimics hypovolemic shock due to massive plasma
  • leakage from microvascular endothelial disruption.
Clinical Features
  • Hypotension (MAP < 65 mmHg, SBP < 90 mmHg)
  • Adrenergic discharge (tachycardia, vasoconstriction)
  • Oliguria (urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/hr)
  • Metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis due to poor perfusion)
  • Mental status changes (obtundation, confusion, lethargy)
  • ECG: ST-T wave changes (suggestive of ischemia due to hypoperfusion)
  • Fever (hyperthermia) or hypothermia (in severe cases)
Differentiation from Hypovolemic Shock:
  • Septic shock → Warm skin (early), later becomes cold & mottled
  • Hypovolemic shock → Cool, clammy skin from the start
Diagnosis
TestFindings
CBCLeukocytosis (or leukopenia in severe cases)
LactateElevated (>2 mmol/L), marker of poor perfusion
Blood culturesIdentify bacterial or fungal infection
CRP, ProcalcitoninElevated in bacterial infections
ABGMetabolic acidosis, high anion gap
Bilirubin, LFTsSuggest hepatic involvement
Creatinine, BUNAcute kidney injury due to shock
PT, PTT, INRDIC evaluation in severe cases
Imaging (CT, US, X-Identifies infection sources (abscess, perforation,
ray)ischemia)
Management
A. Immediate Resuscitation (Sepsis Bundle)
1. Fluids First (30 mL/kg Crystalloids)
  • Lactated Ringer’s (LR) or Normal Saline (NS)
  • Goal: MAP > 65 mmHg, urine output > 0.5 mL/kg/hr
  • Monitor for fluid overload (lung exam, IVC ultrasound)

2. Early Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics (Within 1 Hour)

  • Community-acquired sepsis: Piperacillin-Tazobactam or Cefepime + Metronidazole
  • Hospital-acquired sepsis: Meropenem or Cefepime + Vancomycin
  • Necrotizing soft tissue infections: Vancomycin + Piperacillin- Tazobactam + Clindamycin

3. Vasopressors (If Fluids Fail)

  • First-line: Norepinephrine (maintains perfusion)
  • If persistent hypotension: Add Vasopressin or Epinephrine
  • MAP Goal: Maintain > 65 mmHg
B. Definitive Source Control
1. Surgery for Intra-Abdominal Sepsis
  • Laparotomy for bowel perforation, ischemia, abscess drainage
  • Necrotizing fasciitis: Early debridement, possible amputation

2. Drainage of Infected Fluid Collections

  • Percutaneous drainage for abscesses (CT or US-guided)

3. Debridement of Necrotic Tissue

  • Gangrene, ischemic limbs, infected wounds
C. Supportive ICU Care
1. Oxygenation & Mechanical Ventilation (If needed)
  • For ARDS or respiratory failure

2. Blood Sugar Control

  • Maintain glucose < 180 mg/dL with insulin infusion

3. DVT & Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis

  • Heparin/Enoxaparin (DVT prophylaxis)
  • Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) for GI stress ulcer prevention
High-output Inflammatory (Septic) shock:

High-output inflammatory shock is an early phase of septic shock, characterized by increased cardiac output with systemic vasodilation. It may precede low- output shock or occur after successful resuscitation of low-output shock.

Key Characteristics
  • Hypotension despite high cardiac output
  • Warm, well-perfused extremities (vasodilation)
  • Fever (not always present)
  • High oxygen consumption (1.5x normal)
  • Bounding pulses
  • Wide pulse pressure (SBP − DBP is elevated)
  • Metabolic acidosis due to poor perfusion
Progression to Low-Output Shock

If untreated, progressive vasodilation and capillary leak lead to low cardiac output, cold extremities, and organ failure.

Diagnosis
TestFindings
HemodynamicsHigh CO, Low SVR (Systemic Vascular
Resistance), Low MAP
LactateElevated (>2 mmol/L), marker of anaerobic metabolism
Central Venous Pressure (CVP)Normal or high (unless hypovolemic)
Mixed Venous Oxygen Saturation (SvO₂)High (>75%) due to poor oxygen extraction
EchocardiographyHyperdynamic left ventricle, normal to low
filling pressures
ABGMetabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis)
CRP, ProcalcitoninElevated in bacterial infections
Management
A. Resuscitation
1. Fluids First (Crystalloids)
  • Goal: Optimize preload while avoiding overload
  • Lactated Ringer’s (LR) or Normal Saline (NS), 30 mL/kg IV bolus
  • Monitor: CVP (8–12 mmHg), urine output (>0.5 mL/kg/hr)

2. Optimize Cardiac Function

  • Check ventricular end-diastolic volume (via CVP or echocardiography)
  • If adequate preload → Use inotropes (Dobutamine)
  • If inadequate preload → Give more fluids
3. Avoid Vasoconstrictors (Unless MAP < 65 mmHg)
  • Risk of limb, gut, kidney ischemia
  • Only use vasopressors (Norepinephrine) if fluids & inotropes fail
B. Treat Underlying Cause
1. Early Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics (Within 1 Hour)
  • Community-acquired sepsis: Piperacillin-Tazobactam or Cefepime + Metronidazole
  • Hospital-acquired sepsis: Meropenem or Cefepime + Vancomycin
  • Necrotizing soft tissue infections: Vancomycin + Piperacillin- Tazobactam + Clindamycin

2. Source Control

  • Surgery for bowel perforation, necrosis, abscess drainage
  • Debridement for infected wounds, gangrene
C. Supportive ICU Care
1. Oxygenation & Mechanical Ventilation (If needed)
  • For ARDS or respiratory failure

2. Blood Sugar Control

  • Maintain glucose < 180 mg/dL with insulin infusion

3. DVT & Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis

  • Heparin/Enoxaparin (DVT prophylaxis)
  • Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) for GI stress ulcer prevention
Common physiological responses to shock:
I. Neurohumoral Responses

Shock triggers neurohumoral compensatory mechanisms to maintain circulatory homeostasis and perfusion to vital organs.

1️- Sympathetic Adrenergic Response
  • Vasoconstriction: Arterioles, venules, and small veins (except heart & brain) constrict → ↑ BP & perfusion to heart & brain
  • ↑ Myocardial contractility → Augments cardiac output
  • ↑ Heart rate (tachycardia) → To maintain cardiac output
2️- Hormonal Responses
HormoneFunction in Shock
Angiotensin IIVasoconstriction (skin, kidneys, splanchnic organs) → ↑ BP
& shunts blood to heart & brain. Stimulates aldosterone
release for sodium retention.
Vasopressin (ADH)Constricts peripheral vessels, retains water, and increases blood pressure without reducing kidney perfusion.
CortisolIncreases glucose, reduces inflammation, and enhances
vascular response to catecholamines.
Glucagon & EpinephrineIncreases blood glucose via glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
II. Metabolic Responses
  • Intracellular acidosis → H⁺ exchanged for Na⁺ & Cl⁻ → Cell swelling (~3L intracellular volume gain)
  • Hyperglycemia due to stress hormones → Prevents hypoglycemia, but excess glucose can worsen osmotic diuresis → Avoid glucose-containing fluids in resuscitation
  • Increased plasma oncotic pressure → Draws interstitial fluid back into circulation
III. Microvascular Responses

In severe shock, three pathologic microvascular responses worsen the patient's condition:

1️- Arteriolar Vasodilation & Capillary Leak
  • Loss of vascular tone → Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
  • Plasma extravasation → Fluid shifts into interstitial space → Edema
  • Massive third-spacing in septic shock → Pulmonary, cerebral, or peripheral edema
2️- Endothelial Disruption
  • Inflammatory mediators (cytokines, leukotrienes, thromboxanes, fibrin degradation products, ROS) damage the endothelium.
  • Microvascular thrombosis impairs capillary perfusion, contributing to organ failure.
3️- Microvascular Embolization
  • White cell & platelet aggregates lodge in lungs & liver
  • Triggers further vasodilation & inflammation, worsening capillary leak
IV. Ultrasound in Shock Diagnosis & Resuscitation

Modern noninvasive bedside ultrasound (US) has replaced many invasive monitoring methods (CVP, Swan-Ganz catheters) for shock assessment.

Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (eFAST)
Used in Trauma Patients to Identify:
  • Pericardial effusion (cardiac tamponade)
  • Pneumothorax
  • Intraperitoneal free fluid (hemoperitoneum)
  • Point-of-Care Cardiac Ultrasound in ICU Patients
